title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
summary: A boy spends months learning to understand birds' calls, and uses this skill to warn his village of an approaching storm.
poll: An unusual skill like Hamza's must come from something magical, not patient practice.

versions.title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
versions.text:
A boy lived in a small village. His name was Hamza. He was quiet. He liked birds.

Many birds lived near his home. Hamza sat and listened to them. He did this every day.

At first, all the calls sounded the same. Hamza kept listening. He did this for months.

Slowly, he learned. Some calls meant "danger." Some calls meant "food is here."

Hamza learned to copy some calls. People said, "He can talk to birds!"

But he said, "I just listen. I am not magic."

One day, the birds made a loud, strange call. Many birds flew away fast.

He knew this call. He had heard it once, before a big storm.

He ran home. "A storm is coming!" he said. "The birds told us!"

At first, no one believed him. Then the sky grew dark. A storm came.

The village was safe. People had moved inside. They had tied down loose things.

After the storm, people said thank you. He had not used magic. He had just listened, for a long time.

Hamza liked to sit and listen to the birds. He did this every day. At first, the calls all sounded the same.

Hamza even learned to copy some calls. People in the village began to say, "He can talk to the birds!"

But Hamza always said, "I cannot talk to birds. I have just listened a lot, for a long time."

He had heard this call once before. It came right before a big storm.

He ran home and told his mom. "A storm is coming! The birds are warning us!"

At first, no one did believe him. But soon, the sky grew dark, and a big storm came.

Because Hamza had warned them, the village was ready. People had moved inside and tied down loose things.

After the storm, all the people thanked Hamza. He had not used any magic at all. He had just listened, and learned, for a very long time.

versions.title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
versions.text:
Hamza was a quiet boy who lived in a small village near the edge of the desert. Near his home, many birds lived in the trees and bushes, filling the morning with their calls.

Hamza loved to sit outside and listen to the birds. He did this every day, rain or sun, for a long time. At first, all the calls sounded the same to him, just noise with no clear sense.

But Hamza kept listening for many months, and he did not give up. Slowly, he began to spot small differences in the calls. He learned that one call meant danger was near, while another call meant food had been found.

Hamza even learned to copy some of the calls himself, until he could make a few of them quite well. People in the village began to joke, "Hamza can talk to the birds!"

But Hamza always said, "I cannot really talk to birds. I have just listened a lot, for a long time, until I knew what their sounds meant."

One day, the birds made a loud, strange sound that Hamza had rarely heard before. Many birds flew off fast, all at nearly the same time.

Hamza knew this sound. He had heard it once before, right before a big storm hit the village many months earlier.

He ran home and told his mom and dad. "A storm is coming! Listen—the birds are warning us, just like before."

At first, his folks did not think he was right, since the sky still looked clear. But soon, the sky turned dark, the wind picked up, and a big storm came.

Because Hamza had warned them early, the village had time to get ready. People moved inside and tied down loose things before the storm hit.

After the storm passed, everyone in the village thanked Hamza warmly. He had not used any magic at all. He had just listened, and learned, for a very long time, until he spotted a pattern that most people never noticed.

versions.text:

Hamza loved to sit outside and observe the birds. He listened to every sound they made. He did this every day, and at first, all the calls sounded the same to him, just noise with no clear sense.

But Hamza kept observing and listening for many months. He did not give up, even when his friends teased him for sitting so still. Slowly, he began to spot a pattern in the sounds. He learned that one call meant danger was near, while another call meant food had been found.

Hamza even learned to copy some of the calls himself. People in the village joked that he must be able to talk to the birds. But Hamza always said he could not. He had simply studied their behavior closely enough, for long enough, to know what their sounds meant.

One day, the birds made a loud, strange sound that Hamza had rarely heard before. It was clearly a warning call, and dozens of birds flew off fast, all at once.

Hamza knew this pattern from his memory. He had heard it once before, right before a big storm hit the village. Birds, he thought, could predict such storms before people even noticed.

He ran home and told his family, "A storm is coming! Listen—the birds are warning us, just like before." At first, his family doubted him, since the sky still looked clear. But soon, the sky turned dark, the wind picked up, and a big storm struck the village.

Because Hamza had warned them early, the village had time to get ready. People moved inside, tied down loose things, and brought the animals to shelter before the storm hit.

After the storm passed, everyone in the village thanked Hamza for his timely warning. He had not used any magic at all. He had simply observed, listened, and learned, until he spotted a pattern that most people never noticed.

versions.title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
versions.text:
Hamza was a quiet boy who lived in a small village at the edge of the desert, where the land stretched out flat and dry under a wide open sky. Near his home, many birds lived in the trees and bushes near the well, filling the morning with their calls.

Hamza loved to sit outside for long stretches of time, carefully observing the birds and listening to every sound they made, rather than playing with other children. He did this every day, and at first, all the calls sounded the same to him, just noise with no clear sense.

But Hamza kept observing and listening patiently for many months. He did not give up, even when his friends teased him for sitting so still near the trees. Slowly, he began to spot a pattern in the sounds. He learned that one call meant danger was near, while another call meant food had been found nearby.

Hamza even learned to copy some of the calls himself, until he could make a few of them quite well, much to the delight of the younger children. People in the village joked that he must be able to talk to the birds. But Hamza always said he could not. He had simply studied their behavior closely enough, for long enough, to know what their sounds meant.

One day, the birds made a loud, strange sound that Hamza had rarely heard before. It was clearly a warning call, and dozens of birds flew off fast, all at once, leaving the trees around his home.

Hamza knew this pattern from deep in his memory. He had heard it once before, right before a big storm hit the village many months earlier. Birds, he now thought, could predict such storms before people even noticed anything at all.

He ran home and told his family, "A storm is coming! Listen—the birds are warning us, just like before." At first, his family doubted him, since the sky still looked clear. But soon, the sky turned dark, the wind picked up fast, and a big storm struck the village.

Because Hamza had warned them early, the village had time to get ready. People moved inside, tied down loose things, and brought the animals to shelter before the worst of the storm hit.

After the storm passed, everyone in the village thanked Hamza warmly for his timely warning, even the elders who had doubted him. He had not used any magic at all. He had simply observed, listened, and learned patiently, until he spotted a pattern that most people never noticed.

versions.title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
versions.text:
Hamza was a quiet, meticulous boy who lived in a small village at the edge of the desert, where flat, dry land stretched toward the horizon beneath an open sky. Near his home, several kinds of birds, including sparrows, pigeons, and the occasional falcon, lived in the trees and bushes near the well, filling each morning with their calls.

Hamza loved spending long stretches of time outdoors, carefully observing the birds and listening to every sound they made, rather than playing with other children his age. He did this meticulously every day, and at first, all the calls sounded the same to him, nothing more than noise without any clear meaning.

But Hamza kept observing and listening patiently for many months, never once giving up, even when his friends teased him for sitting so still near the trees. Slowly, he began to recognize a pattern in the sounds. He discovered that one call signaled danger was near, while another call meant food had been found nearby, and yet another seemed to summon distant birds closer.

Hamza even practiced copying some of the calls himself, until he could imitate a few of them quite well, much to the delight of the village's younger children. Many villagers, somewhat skeptical at first, joked that he must possess some power to talk with birds, but Hamza always corrected them: he could not truly talk to birds, he explained, since he had simply studied their behavior closely enough, over a long enough time, to anticipate what their sounds actually meant.

One afternoon, the birds suddenly made an urgent, unfamiliar sound that Hamza had rarely heard before. It was unmistakably a warning call, and dozens of birds scattered away almost at once, abandoning the trees around his home.

Hamza recognized this pattern from somewhere deep in his memory. He had heard a similar warning once before, right before a powerful storm had struck the village many months earlier, and he now understood that birds could apparently anticipate such weather long before any person could.

He hurried home and told his family, "A storm is approaching! Listen—the birds are warning us again, exactly as they did before." At first, his family remained skeptical, since the sky overhead still looked completely clear. However, within the hour, the sky darkened, the wind grew stronger, and a powerful storm struck the village.

Because Hamza had given his warning early, the villagers had time to prepare. People moved indoors, secured loose items, and brought their animals safely to shelter before the storm's worst conditions arrived.

After the storm passed, every villager thanked Hamza sincerely for his timely forecast, including the very elders who had doubted him at first. He had relied on no magic whatsoever. He had simply observed, listened, and learned with patience, until he detected a natural phenomenon that almost no one else around him had ever paused to notice.

versions.title: The Boy Who Talked to Birds
versions.text:
Hamza was a quiet, meticulous boy who lived in a small village at the edge of the desert, where flat, dry land stretched endlessly toward the horizon beneath an unbroken open sky. Near his home, several kinds of birds, including sparrows, pigeons, and the occasional swift-winged falcon, lived in the trees and bushes near the well, filling each morning with their calls, which most villagers barely noticed at all, treating it as ordinary background noise rather than a genuinely meaningful source of information about the world unfolding around them.

Hamza, by sharp contrast, loved spending long, uninterrupted stretches of time outdoors, carefully observing the birds and listening attentively to every sound they produced, rather than playing with other children his age; he did this meticulously every single day, and at first, all the calls sounded entirely identical to him, nothing more than noise without any discernible meaning whatsoever. Yet he kept observing and listening patiently for many months, never once abandoning his quiet study despite the teasing of friends who could not understand why anyone would sit so motionless near the trees for hours at a time, and gradually he began recognizing distinct, recurring patterns in the sounds, discovering that one call signaled approaching danger, while another call indicated that food had been found nearby, and yet another seemed to summon distant birds closer together.

Hamza even practiced reproducing some of these calls himself, until he could imitate them quite convincingly, much to the delight of the village's younger children; many villagers, understandably skeptical at first, joked that he must possess some unusual power to talk with birds, but Hamza always corrected them patiently, insisting that he could not genuinely talk to birds, since he had simply studied their behavior closely enough, over a sufficiently long period, to anticipate what their sounds actually, consistently meant.

One afternoon, the birds abruptly produced an urgent, wholly unfamiliar sound that Hamza had rarely, if ever, heard before; it was unmistakably a warning call, and dozens of birds scattered away almost simultaneously, abandoning the trees around his home entirely and without hesitation. Hamza recognized this particular pattern from somewhere deep within his memory, having heard a remarkably similar warning once before, immediately preceding a powerful storm that had struck the village many months earlier, and he now understood, with growing certainty, that birds could apparently anticipate such weather phenomena, relying on no instrument whatsoever, long before any human observer possibly could.

He hurried home at once and told his family urgently, "A storm is approaching! Listen closely—the birds are warning us again, exactly as they did before." Initially, his family remained thoroughly skeptical, since the sky overhead still appeared completely clear with nothing unusual in sight, but within the hour, the sky darkened with surprising speed, the wind intensified sharply, and a powerful storm ultimately struck the village regardless of their earlier doubts.

Because Hamza had issued his warning sufficiently early, the villagers had more than enough time to prepare thoroughly; people moved indoors, secured loose items throughout their properties, and brought their animals safely to shelter well before the storm's worst conditions finally arrived. Few natural phenomena illustrate so clearly how patient, meticulous observation of the surrounding world can rival even modern, instrument-based forecasting: Hamza's warning, built entirely on months of careful, deliberate listening rather than any mechanical instrument, proved just as accurate as the storm itself ultimately, undeniably turned out to be.

After the storm eventually passed, every villager thanked Hamza sincerely and repeatedly for his timely forecast, including the very elders who had doubted him most firmly at first. He had relied on no magic whatsoever; he had simply observed, listened, and learned with remarkable, sustained patience, over an extended period, until he detected a natural phenomenon that almost no one else around him had ever once paused to notice.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: A boy who secretly has a magic power over birds and trees in the forest
A boy who listens to birds and warns his village of a storm
A village that gets destroyed by a terrible storm and has to move away
A single bird that teaches people how to fly away from danger
questions.why: The article tells how Hamza listens to birds for months and uses what he learns to warn his village of a storm.

wrong.A: The article says Hamza does not have a magic power.
wrong.C: The village is not destroyed; it prepares in time.
wrong.D: No bird teaches people to fly in the story.

questions.stem: What did Hamza do every day for many months?
options: He fed the hungry birds bread every single morning
He built many small nests for the birds to use
He raced the fast birds across the whole village
He listened very carefully to the birds' calls
questions.why: The article says Hamza sat and listened to the birds every single day for many months.

wrong.A: The article does not mention feeding the birds.
wrong.B: The article does not mention building nests.
wrong.C: The article does not mention racing birds.

questions.stem: What did Hamza learn that some bird calls meant?
options: That danger was near or food had been found
That it was time for everyone to sleep
That rain would never ever come again
That the birds wanted to race each other
questions.why: The article says Hamza learned that some calls meant danger was near and others meant food had been found.

wrong.B: The calls were not about sleep.
wrong.C: The calls were not about rain never coming.
wrong.D: The calls were not about racing.

questions.stem: What did Hamza do right after he heard the birds make the warning sound?
options: He quietly went back to sleep again
He chased the loud birds far away
He ran home and told his family
He built a brand-new nest instead
questions.why: After hearing the warning sound, Hamza ran home right away and told his family a storm was coming.

wrong.A: Hamza did not go back to sleep.
wrong.B: Hamza did not chase the birds.
wrong.D: Hamza did not build a nest.

questions.stem: Why did the village get ready for the storm in time?
options: Hamza warned his family after hearing the birds
The sky had stayed dark for many days before
A radio had announced the coming storm in the village
The birds built shelters for the people of the village
questions.why: Because Hamza warned his family after hearing the birds, the village had time to prepare before the storm hit.

wrong.B: The sky was clear at first, not dark for days.
wrong.C: The article does not mention a radio.
wrong.D: The birds did not build shelters.

questions.stem: In the article, the word storm means —
options: a quiet, sunny day with no clouds at all
a special kind of loud bird call in the trees
a strong weather event with wind and rain
a soft type of nest made of grass and twigs
questions.why: The article describes the storm as a time when the sky grew dark and strong weather arrived.

wrong.A: A storm is not a quiet, sunny day.
wrong.B: A storm is not a kind of bird call.
wrong.D: A storm is not a type of nest.

questions.stem: Why did Hamza say he could not really talk to birds?
options: Because he was too shy to admit his power to them
Because the birds could not understand him at all
Because he was secretly afraid of birds and their noise
Because he had only listened and learned, not used magic
questions.why: Hamza explains that he simply listened and learned for a long time, rather than using any kind of magic.

wrong.A: Hamza was not hiding a power; he had none.
wrong.B: The article does not say the birds could not understand him.
wrong.C: Hamza was not afraid of birds.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Hamza from how he spent his time?
options: He was patient and liked to watch things
He disliked being outside in the sun
He mostly wanted to become famous
He was afraid of loud storms
questions.why: Hamza spent months sitting quietly and listening closely, which shows he was patient and observant.

wrong.B: Hamza loved being outside with the birds.
wrong.C: The article does not say Hamza wanted fame.
wrong.D: Hamza was not described as afraid of storms.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Hamza's village was lucky that he listened to the birds? Explain using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Hamza's village was lucky that he listened to the birds. Because he had listened to them for many months, he knew their warning call and ran home to tell his family. The village then had time to move inside and cover their things before the storm arrived.

keyWords.definition: to watch something carefully and closely
keyWords.example: Scientists observe animals in the wild without disturbing them.

keyWords.definition: something that happens in the same way again and again, so it can be noticed
keyWords.example: She noticed a pattern in the numbers and could guess what came next.

keyWords.definition: a sign or signal that tells people something dangerous might happen
keyWords.example: The loud siren was a warning that everyone should leave the building.

keyWords.definition: the way a person or animal acts
keyWords.example: The zookeeper studied the lion's behavior every afternoon.

keyWords.definition: to say what you think will happen before it happens
keyWords.example: Based on the clouds, she could predict that it would rain soon.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Hamza used a secret magical power to control the birds of the village
By observing bird calls, Hamza learned a pattern that warned of a storm
Birds in the village only ate food that Hamza gave them each day
The storm destroyed every single house in the village by the sea
questions.why: The article shows that Hamza's careful observation of bird behavior let him recognize a warning pattern before the storm.

wrong.A: The article explicitly says Hamza used no magic.
wrong.C: The article does not say Hamza fed the birds.
wrong.D: The village prepared and was not destroyed.

questions.stem: What convinced the villagers that Hamza might be right about the coming storm?
options: A scientist had confirmed his early prediction
The birds had returned and spoken to the villagers
The sky darkened and the wind picked up soon after
Hamza's uncle had told everyone to trust him fully
questions.why: The article says that within the hour, the sky darkened and the wind picked up, matching Hamza's warning.

wrong.A: No scientist appears in the story.
wrong.B: Birds do not speak to villagers.
wrong.D: Hamza's uncle is not mentioned in this story.

questions.stem: What had Hamza heard before, right before the earlier storm months earlier?
options: A loud, unfamiliar warning call much like this one
Thunder rumbling faintly from somewhere far away
A cheerful song sung by his favorite bird
Nothing at all that seemed unusual that day
questions.why: The article says Hamza remembered a similar warning call from right before the earlier storm.

wrong.B: The article does not mention distant thunder as the earlier sign.
wrong.C: The article does not mention a favorite song.
wrong.D: He did notice something unusual: the warning call.

questions.stem: Why did many villagers assume Hamza could talk to birds?
options: Because he could imitate several of their calls well
Because he had told them he had magic powers
Because the birds always followed him everywhere
Because he liked to wear real bird feathers
questions.why: Because Hamza had practiced and could imitate bird calls, villagers joked that he could talk to birds.

wrong.B: Hamza always denied having magic powers.
wrong.C: The article does not say birds followed him everywhere.
wrong.D: The article does not mention feathers.

questions.stem: In the article, the word behavior most nearly means —
options: a type of storm with strong winds
the way an animal acts or does things
a kind of nest built high in a tree
a sudden, unexpected warning sound
questions.why: Hamza studied the birds' behavior, meaning the way they acted, to understand their calls.

wrong.A: Behavior is not a type of storm.
wrong.C: Behavior is not a kind of nest.
wrong.D: Behavior is not a sound itself.

questions.stem: Why was Hamza able to recognize the danger before anyone else in the village?
options: He had studied the birds' patterns closely enough to notice something
He owned a very special weather radio that told him about every storm
An elder had told him about it in advance, in a story at night
He simply guessed randomly and got lucky, as he did every day
questions.why: Hamza's months of careful study let him recognize the unusual warning pattern before anyone else noticed it.

wrong.B: There is no radio in the story.
wrong.C: No elder warned Hamza in advance.
wrong.D: His recognition came from study, not a random guess.

questions.stem: What does the villagers' initial doubt about Hamza's warning suggest?
options: They trusted him completely from the very start
They did not expect a boy to predict weather so well
They thought birds could not make sounds at all
They believed only village elders could study animals
questions.why: The villagers doubted Hamza at first because they did not expect a boy's careful observation to outperform their own sense of the weather.

wrong.A: They doubted him at first, not trusted him immediately.
wrong.C: They knew birds made sounds; they just doubted the warning's meaning.
wrong.D: The article does not say only elders can study animals.

questions.stem: How is Hamza's explanation for his 'ability' different from what the villagers first assumed?
options: Villagers guessed magic; Hamza said it was patient study
Villagers thought he was lying, and he agreed he was
Villagers assumed a book taught him, and he agreed
Villagers thought birds taught him their language, and he agreed
questions.why: Villagers joked about magic, but Hamza always corrected them, explaining his skill came from patient study, not magic.

wrong.C: The article does not mention a book.
wrong.D: Hamza did not agree the birds taught him a language.

MID.prompt: Explain how Hamza learned to understand the birds' calls, and why this helped his village. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how Hamza learned to understand the birds.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Hamza learned to understand the birds' calls by observing and listening to them patiently for many months. He noticed a pattern: one call meant danger, another meant food had been found. This careful study helped his village because when the birds suddenly made an unfamiliar warning call, Hamza recognized it from before a past storm and warned his family in time, letting the whole village prepare before the storm struck.

keyWords.definition: extremely careful and paying attention to every small detail
keyWords.example: The meticulous scientist recorded every measurement twice to be sure.

keyWords.definition: to expect or sense that something will happen before it does
keyWords.example: Experienced sailors anticipate storms by watching the changing sky.

keyWords.definition: a statement about what is likely to happen in the future, especially the weather
keyWords.example: The weather forecast warned people about heavy rain this weekend.

keyWords.definition: something that happens or exists, especially something unusual or hard to explain
keyWords.example: A rainbow is a natural phenomenon caused by sunlight and rain.

keyWords.definition: not easily convinced; having doubts about whether something is true
keyWords.example: The skeptical reporter asked for proof before printing the story.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: Hamza possessed a supernatural power to speak with birds
Hamza's careful observation let him sense a storm coming
Birds are generally dangerous animals villagers should avoid
Forecasting weather is impossible without modern instruments
questions.why: The article shows that Hamza's meticulous, patient observation of bird calls let him anticipate the storm before anyone else.

wrong.A: The article explicitly denies that Hamza had any supernatural power.
wrong.C: The article does not portray birds as dangerous to avoid.
wrong.D: Hamza's own forecast, without instruments, proved accurate.

questions.stem: In the article, the word phenomenon most nearly means —
options: a particular kind of common village bird
a specific type of dark, heavy storm cloud
a simple game that children in the village play
an observable event, especially one hard to explain
questions.why: Hamza detected a natural phenomenon, meaning an observable occurrence, that most people never noticed.

wrong.A: Phenomenon is not a kind of bird.
wrong.B: Phenomenon is not a type of cloud.
wrong.C: Phenomenon is not a children's game.

questions.stem: According to the article, what kinds of birds lived near Hamza's home?
options: Only large eagles and hunting hawks
Sparrows, pigeons, and occasionally falcons
Colorful parrots and strutting peacocks
Only plain gray pigeons near the well
questions.why: The article names sparrows, pigeons, and the occasional falcon as the birds living near Hamza's home.

wrong.A: Eagles and hawks are not mentioned.
wrong.C: Parrots and peacocks are not mentioned.
wrong.D: More than just pigeons are named.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why the villagers were initially skeptical of Hamza's warning?
options: They simply did not like Hamza personally
They thought birds could not fly during storms
The sky still looked clear, so no evidence yet existed
They had never once seen a clear sky turn stormy
questions.why: The article says the sky still looked completely clear, giving the villagers no visible reason yet to believe a storm was coming.

wrong.A: There is no evidence of personal dislike for Hamza.
wrong.B: The article does not discuss birds flying during storms.
wrong.D: A clear sky turning stormy is not described as unprecedented for them.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize that Hamza used no magic at all?
options: To clarify that his skill came from patient observation
To suggest that his achievement is less impressive than it seems
To hint that the storm was not actually a real one
To imply that the birds themselves are magical creatures
questions.why: The article repeatedly clarifies that Hamza's skill came from patient observation, not magic, to make its lesson about effort and attention clear.

wrong.B: The article presents his skill as impressive precisely because it was earned through effort.
wrong.C: The storm clearly and genuinely occurred in the story.
wrong.D: The article denies any magical explanation.

questions.stem: What allowed Hamza to anticipate the coming storm before anyone else noticed?
options: A lucky coincidence that had no real explanation
His long study of the birds' calls and behavior
A direct warning given by the village elders
Advanced weather equipment that he had built himself
questions.why: The article explains that his months of meticulous study revealed a recognizable warning pattern in the birds' calls.

wrong.A: His recognition is explained as skill, not coincidence.
wrong.C: No village elder warned him in advance.
wrong.D: Hamza used no equipment at all.

questions.stem: How does Hamza's method of 'forecasting' the storm differ from relying on modern weather instruments?
options: It relies on no observation of nature at all
It depends on observing a natural signal, not machines
It requires costly equipment only scientists can use
It can never be accurate under any circumstances
questions.why: Hamza's forecast relied on observing birds' behavior directly, rather than on any mechanical weather instrument.

wrong.A: Hamza's method is based entirely on close observation of nature.
wrong.C: Hamza used no expensive equipment at all.
wrong.D: His forecast turned out to be accurate.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the villagers thanking Hamza at the end, including those who had doubted him?
options: To show that patience and observation can earn trust
To suggest that Hamza should be treated as a magician
To indicate that the village elders deserved no respect
To imply that birds should be formally honored in the village
questions.why: Showing even the skeptical elders thanking Hamza emphasizes how patient, careful observation ultimately proved its worth.

wrong.B: The article explicitly rejects a magical explanation for Hamza's skill.
wrong.C: The elders are not mocked; they are shown changing their minds respectfully.
wrong.D: The article does not suggest formally honoring the birds.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says an unusual skill like Hamza's must come from something magical, not patient practice. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Hamza.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that an unusual skill like Hamza's must come from something magical. The story explains clearly that Hamza spent many months meticulously observing birds and listening to their calls before he could recognize any patterns, and he always corrected villagers who joked about magic. Someone might argue that predicting a storm from bird calls still sounds impossible for an ordinary person, but the article shows his forecast came from recognizing a specific warning pattern he had heard once before, not from any supernatural power. His success proves that patient, careful practice can produce results that look magical without actually being magical at all.
